title: Endeavour Shuttle Lands at New Home: California Science Center Unveils Exhibit in LA Parks
body:
Los Angeles welcomed a new landmark on Friday as the California Science Center unveiled the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, a sprawling exhibition hall that now houses the retired space shuttle Endeavour. The 200‑foot‑long orbiter, freshly restored and positioned on a custom‑built platform, became the centerpiece of the museum’s most ambitious expansion to date, drawing crowds eager to step inside a piece of modern history that once carried astronauts into orbit.

The Oschin Center, which adds roughly 200,000 square feet to the existing campus, represents the culmination of a decade‑long planning effort and a $150 million public‑private partnership. Architects designed the structure to echo the sleek lines of aerospace engineering while providing flexible gallery spaces for rotating exhibits. Visitors can now trace the shuttle’s 25‑year career—from its first flight in 1992 to its final mission in 2011—through interactive displays that blend archival footage, astronaut testimonies, and hands‑on science activities. The exhibit also incorporates a “Mission Control” simulation, allowing guests to experience the high‑stakes decision‑making that defined each launch.

Endeavour’s arrival marks the first time a shuttle has been displayed in a fully indoor environment since the retirement of the fleet in 2011. Previously, the orbiter was housed in a temporary outdoor pavilion that exposed it to the elements and limited visitor access. The new climate‑controlled hall not only protects the shuttle’s delicate thermal‑protective tiles and aluminum skin but also offers a 360‑degree viewing experience, with walk‑through tunnels that let guests walk beneath the nose and along the side cargo bay. Curators emphasize that the immersive layout is intended to inspire the next generation of engineers, scientists, and explorers by showcasing the engineering marvels that made human spaceflight possible.

Beyond the shuttle itself, the center expands the Science Center’s educational mission. The Oschin facility includes a state‑of‑the‑art planetarium, a “Future of Flight” gallery featuring electric aircraft and autonomous drones, and a research lab where students can engage in real‑time data analysis from current NASA missions. Partnerships with local schools and university programs are already in place, with a schedule of workshops that align with STEM curricula. Officials hope the venue will serve as a catalyst for Los Angeles County’s growing aerospace sector, which has seen a resurgence in private‑sector investment and a surge in satellite‑launch startups.

The opening also carries symbolic weight for the city’s broader cultural landscape. Situated in Exposition Park, adjacent to the Natural History Museum and the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, the new center reinforces the area’s identity as a hub of public education and civic pride. City leaders view the project as a boost to tourism, projecting an increase of 1.5 million visitors annually, and as a catalyst for economic development in surrounding neighborhoods. Moreover, the presence of Endeavour—a vehicle that once carried the first American woman to walk in space and the first African‑American astronaut to command a shuttle—underscores Los Angeles’ commitment to diversity and inclusion in the sciences.

Looking ahead, the California Science Center plans to rotate additional artifacts from NASA’s storied past, including lunar modules, satellite prototypes, and a collection of astronaut suits. Long‑term, the institution aims to host traveling exhibitions that spotlight emerging space initiatives such as Artemis lunar missions and commercial orbital ventures. As the shuttle’s wings stretch over the Oschin Center’s glass‑clad facade, it serves as a tangible reminder that the era of human spaceflight is far from over; rather, it is poised to enter a new chapter, with Los Angeles positioned at the forefront of inspiring curiosity and fostering the talent that will carry humanity beyond Earth’s orbit.
